Leonida exists within Grand Theft Auto VI, a buzzy  Read more...   The post  Your Riches Are Stored Up in Leonida  appeared first on  Christianity Today .

title_zh: 在LGBT+的世界中栽培下一代
content: The world has a lot to say to the next generation about identity and sexuality. In a culture filled with competing messages, how can we faithfully teach children the truth while also modeling love and compassion toward those who have rejected it? In this session from TGCW26, Betsy Childs Howard interviews Rachel Gilson about how to talk to the next generation about issues of sexuality with love, clarity, and gospel-centered confidence. In This Episode 00:00 – Rachel Gilson’s journey to faith 04:06 – Discovering Jesus and early Christian walk 10:13 – Parenting and teaching sexuality 16:25 – Theological foundations for teaching sexuality 31:16 – Addressing sexual brokenness and false gospels 35:36 – Handling complicated situations 45:24 – Loving across differences 47:59 – Practical advice for parents 48:31 – Prayer and closing remarks Resources Mentioned: Arlo Takes Off by Betsy Childs Howard Born Again This Way by Rachel Gilson Parenting Without Panic by Rachel Gilson Mere Christianity by C. title: How to Fire Someone at a Christian Organization
summary: If managers do their jobs well, believe that God is sovereign, and bring the love of Christ even into hard conversations, everyone will be better off.
summary_zh: 无论是辅导经理、上游规划、接听电话、还是安排裁员。 每次都是艰难的。 与员工分离是经理最重的事情之一。 这样做既明确又友好,需要大量的准备和情绪调节.
title_zh: 如何在基督教组织中解雇某人
content: Over the course of my career, I’ve participated in more than 190 exits of employees, whether I was coaching a manager, planning upstream, sitting in on calls, or orchestrating layoffs. Each time was tough. Parting ways with an employee is one of the heaviest things a manager does. Doing it both clearly and kindly takes a lot of preparation and emotional regulation. In a faith-based workplace, these decisions can be even more surprising and hurtful, because managers try to spare the discomfort of a conversation about performance under any number of banners of being “kind.” How should we think about this as Christians who manage other Christians? Why Good Work Is Important A church’s mission is to spread the good news of Jesus, create ways for people to know him more deeply, and love our neighbors. A Christian nonprofit’s purpose is adjacent—to provide mercy, justice, evangelism, or discipleship while pointing people to Christ and their local church. This work happens through ministry and outreach staff, but also through effective operations. Doing this work takes all types of roles: pastors, administrators, and ministry coordinators; managers, accountants, and musicians; executive admins, facilities operators, and IT teams. Much of what it takes to run a church or Christian organization happens outside the hours of direct ministry. To do any of this well, churches and nonprofits must hire capable people who can effectively perform their duties and steward the mission. When managers in a secular workplace don’t hire wisely, I’ve seen the result in poor functional performance, departmental infighting, disengagement, acrimonious exits, and abuse of company resources. In a faith-based organization or church, you may get a mix of this and something worse: the spread of the gospel can be compromised too. Upstream Work for Managers As a manager, if you notice someone isn’t performing well, the best time to start talking about it isn’t at the exit conversation. It’s way upstream from that. Your core job is to ensure your people have what they need to be successful. That includes clear expectations, communication of what success looks like, feedback on performance, and accountability for meeting those standards. Ideally, you’re doing these on a regular basis in one-on-one meetings  and in performance check-ins throughout the year. Churches and nonprofits must hire capable people who can effectively perform their duties and steward the mission. This is a manager’s job, and faith-based organizations don’t have a softer standard. Where I’ve seen termination decisions and conversations go south—in Christian organizations or elsewhere—is when a manager doesn’t understand this. (Or, worse, they understand it but think that somehow it doesn’t apply to them.) Speaking to an employee about parting ways because you’ve consistently documented underperformance is a rough conversation. It’s far worse when your failure to give regular feedback leaves an employee blindsided, confused, and hurt when you need to broach termination. Often, that failure is rooted in a desire to avoid conflict or hurt feelings. The manager would rather spare himself the discomfort of a direct conversation. In a Christian organization, this impulse pulls hard. The employees under your care all love Jesus. They’re there to promote the church’s mission and spread the gospel. You may even sit shoulder to shoulder in the pews with them on Sundays. But James 4:17 has a word for managers who fail to do the difficult work: “Whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin.” Colossians 4:1 underlines this: “Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.” I’ve watched managers avoid the perceived sin of commission (telling someone he’s doing a poor job in his role) and step right into the sin of omission (letting the problem fester until the employee is struggling and a termination conversation seems inevitable). It doesn’t have to be this way. The hard thing and the loving thing aren’t at odds here. Justice, Mercy, and God’s Sovereignty at Work Let’s say you have an employee you’ve been coaching and providing with direct feedback about his (or her) performance. You’ve clearly communicated his responsibilities, warned him when he’s failed, given chances for improvement, and clarified what good performance looks like. It’s not a situation of grave moral failure or breach of ethics, just run-of-the-mill underperformance. What if he doesn’t improve? Are churches or Christian organizations allowed to fire someone for something besides moral failure? Is it fair to let someone go because he isn’t good at his church job? The short answer: Yes. Faith-based organizations hire people to perform a set of roles and responsibilities that contribute to the thriving of that organization. This means doing the job satisfactorily, abiding by the organization’s codes of conduct, and operating within legal bounds of employment. When someone—regardless of his intentions—fails to consistently meet these expectations, parting ways is a course of action that’s on the table. That’s not callous; it’s a means to preserve the integrity of the organization’s mission. But letting someone go should be a last resort . Managers can and should be sensitive to giving clear direction and expectations, continual feedback on what’s going well (or not), and a reasonable timeline to make improvements. And sometimes—for legal or other reasons—someone will need reasonable accommodations to get his work done. We need to give people as fair of a shot as possible to succeed. The worst situation for everyone is where a person is struggling, and the manager hasn’t done anything to intervene because a manager thinks his silent toleration is showing “mercy.” That behavior isn’t justice or mercy—it’s abdicating responsibility as a steward of your employees and your organization’s mission. But let’s say the manager has done his best to set clear expectations, addressed flagging performance, or provided reasonable accommodations. The employee still doesn’t seem to ever improve. What then? As managers, it’s easy to worry that termination ruins someone’s life. It’s tempting to want to avoid that conversation and to keep giving him chances to get better (even if he’s shown that’s not possible). But this can become a way to protect the manager from discomfort and a hard decision; it does nothing to benefit the employee. Silent toleration isn’t justice or mercy—it’s abdicating responsibility as a steward of your employees and your organization’s mission. When we hold back the hard call, we tell ourselves a story about mercy: I don’t want to be the one who upends this person’s life, so I won’t go there. That’s a heavy burden to put on your shoulders. To believe you’re ruining someone’s life by ending his employment is to believe you hold his future in your hands. But here’s the thing: You don’t. You aren’t sovereign over this person’s story. You cannot see his next chapter. The assumption that you can, that keeping him in a role where he’s failing is protecting him from some fate only you can foresee, isn’t humility. It’s pride. We’re obligated to be fair and right and just to the employees in our care (Prov. 2:9, 21:15; Mic. 6:8). Sometimes that means the consequences of one person’s poor behavior at work have to be addressed through parting ways. Remember that God also sees our work, and in his grace he often allows us to suffer the just consequences of our actions. We likewise need to be fair in managing performance even if that involves a hard call. Sometimes, letting a person go who isn’t performing is a boon to him long-term. It can be the catalyst to propel him to a future role or career where his abilities are better fit for what another organization needs. author: Andrew Smith

title: Modernity Is Seeking a Hypergood. It’s Making Us Miserable.
summary: Why does modernity feel unlivable? Because secularism has its own versions of monotheism and polytheism.
summary_zh: 查尔斯·泰勒(Charles Taylor)在其著作"自我的来源"(Source of the Self)中认为,道德框架是多种多样的,是不可避免的. 没有一个中立的人能从距离和客观的角度, 来调查其他人的道德框架, 以及他们的偏见, 似乎不受自己道德框架的影响。 我们都有 从生命的开始,我们便开始适应特定的道德框架。 通过它们,我们构建了我们的身份,作为本身是道德空间的叙述。
title_zh: 现代性正在追求一种超善。它让我们痛苦不堪。
content: In his book Sources of the Self , Charles Taylor argues that moral frameworks are diverse and inescapable. There’s no neutral human being who can survey everyone else’s moral frameworks, with all their biases, from a position of distance and objectivity, as though untouched by a moral framework of his own. We all have them. From the beginning of life, we intuit particular moral frameworks. Through them, we construct our identities as narratives that are themselves moral spaces. Alongside this, as modern Western people, we treat the sense of self as a moral source in its own right. Whereas some cultures imagine esteem and validation to come from other people on the basis of our deeds (“You are a good person because you did . . .”), Western culture gives us a mantra of unconditional self-affirmation (“I am a good person because I say so”) even when the content our lives suggests otherwise. How should Christians in the West think about that local moral framework? In an important sense, it shows us we aren’t the only ones who think about our lives in terms of justification and sanctification. Rather, our secular neighbors live within secularized versions of those categories . Their sense of self makes a qualitative judgment that while life contains many goods, one good must rank highest. Alignment with that highest good is a powerful thing. It confers a justifying power on me, grounding my identity in something good. Having identified myself with that good, though, a hard and personal question necessarily follows: How does my actual life shape up with that highest good? In a secularized sense, Western culture teaches us to assess our “sanctification” in view of our “justification.” This framework makes sense of Taylor’s claim that all modern people are invested in counterparts to these deeply Christian notions. Beyond this, it also raises a prior question: How do modern Westernized people arrive at a highest good in the first place? Without a highest good, you have no standard by which to lay hold of justification or to measure your sanctification. Taylor’s work offers several lenses for answering that question, much like the lenses an optometrist combines in a refraction machine to produce a sharp image. Let’s focus on one of them: Taylor’s idea of the hypergood. The modern self arrives at its highest good by taking a finite, ordinary good and asking it to play the role of an ultimate one. Read alongside Augustine’s distinction between use and enjoyment , Taylor’s concept reveals this move as a form of idolatry. It overburdens the goods we elevate, damages the goods we neglect, and sets us in conflict with others and with ourselves. Only when the ultimate place belongs to God can ordinary goods be freed to be what they are. Why the ‘Good Life’ Is Hard to Define In chapter 3 of Sources of the Self , “Ethics of Inarticulacy,” Taylor argues that modern Western people find the concept of the “good life” difficult to grasp, for several reasons. Our identities have many layers that feed into and out of one another in ways that are hard to put into words. We recognize some of those layers as universal, such as abstract political or ideological commitments that also form the others people’s identities. We recognize other layers as highly particular to ourselves. I might share the same political label as you do, but you didn’t grow up in my town, in my family, or in my skin, and your experiences aren’t my experiences. Holding those two things together is an exceptionally burdensome task. The modern self arrives at its highest good by taking a finite, ordinary good and asking it to play the role of an ultimate one. Our present-day identities are also shaped by long and complex historical developments we struggle to narrate, or about which we are simply oblivious. Imagine being asked “What does it mean for you to be a British Christian?” and beginning your answer with “Well, around the year AD 600, Aethelberht, pagan king of Kent, converted to Christianity . . .” A year of solid talking later, you finally arrive at your life in 2026. Or imagine not even beginning with Aethelberht but with the words “Let us begin with the Homeric man.” That isn’t what we tend to do. Taylor identifies another factor in the ethics of inarticulacy, one he develops more fully in A Secular Age : the difference between living in a transcendent frame and living in an immanent frame. Sources of the Self represents a preparatory stage for that distinction, but the distinction is already emerging there. Consider a pre-Enlightenment, pre-Cartesian, premodern person, such as a medieval European. He experiences his sense of self in such a way that he believes his mind conforms to things, rather than things conforming to his mind. His moral framework intuits that all things are imbued with inherent meaning and sacred order and that the cosmos as a whole exists in relation to an order that exceeds it. This is life within a transcendent frame. It orients life around a proper distinction between many things that are relative and the one thing that is ontologically ultimate. The ultimate is categorically different from ordinary, nonultimate things. In Christian terms, this expresses the distinction between the Creator and the creature: One is ultimate, and the other is relative. In A Secular Age , Taylor traces the shift from medieval to modern as a shift from life in a transcendent frame to life in an immanent frame. In an immanent frame, things conform to my mind, and my sense of self is fundamentally buffered from my body, from my physical environment, and from any claims of metaphysical reality. The way I distinguish ultimate things from ordinary things is transformed as well, because the ultimate is no longer transcendent. It’s immanent. The ultimate as a categorically other, transcendent reality is gone. What happens instead is that I take something from the immanent realm, from the things near to me, and make it act as my ultimate thing. Taylor sees this as inescapable for the modern self: We all have something that takes ultimate place. He uses the language of “the thing you’d be at sea without.” If this thing weren’t holding my identity together, I couldn’t be me. I would be lost. The central question, then, is how does the modern secularized self, which Taylor elsewhere calls the buffered self in an immanent frame, arrive at a highest good? Taylor gives us a particularly useful lens. Taylor and the Hypergood Taylor introduces the idea of the hypergood in chapter 3 of Sources of the Self and continues to develop it in chapter 4, “Moral Sources.” Two caveats are in order. First, the hypergood appears only in Sources of the Self . Taylor doesn’t reprise it in subsequent works. Second, scholars of Taylor’s works have read the concept in different ways. Charles Blattberg, for instance, argues that hypergood is an underdeveloped concept within the book. My own reading is far closer to that of the Dutch philosopher Jasper van Buuren . The idea works like this: Everyone lives within a moral framework, however much we struggle to articulate it, and nobody lives within a moral framework free of value judgments. No one is an absolute relativist who finds every good to be equally important, because life isn’t livable that way. Life requires us to find some things more important than others. Without that, we would be completely overwhelmed and paralyzed by the multiplicity of the world. Our sense of agency would end, and we would become entirely passive, acted on but unable to act. In practice, modern people don’t generally live like this. Taylor describes how modern people often hold a hierarchy of increasingly important goods. For some, the high-ranking goods will be the ideal of rational self-mastery, family life, self-expression, or fame. He writes, Most of us not only live with many goods but find that we have to rank them, and in some cases, this ranking makes one of them of supreme importance
content_zh:
查尔斯·泰勒(Charles Taylor)在其著作"自我的来源"(Source of the Self)中认为,道德框架是多种多样的,是不可避免的. 没有一个中立的人能从距离和客观的角度, 来调查其他人的道德框架, 以及他们的偏见, 似乎不受自己道德框架的影响。 我们都有 从生命的开始,我们便开始适应特定的道德框架。
通过它们,我们构建了我们的身份,作为本身是道德空间的叙述。 与此同时,我们作为现代的西方人,将自我感作为道德来源。 虽然有些文化认为尊敬和认可来自他人,
西方文化给了我们一个无条件自我肯定的口号(“我是一个好人,因为我这样说”),即使我们的生活内容表明并非如此。 西方基督徒应该如何思考这个当地道德框架? 从重要的意义上讲,它向我们展示了我们并非唯一一个在理性和神圣化方面思考我们生活的人。
相反,我们的世俗邻居生活在这些类别的世俗版本中。 他们的自我意识做出了质的判断:虽然生活包含着许多商品,但一件好事必须排到最高. 与最高利益一致是一件很强大的事情。 它赋予我一个正当的权力, 将我的身份建立在一件好事上。
然而,我认同了这一点,因此,一个困难而个人的问题必然如下: 我真正的生命是如何 与最高的好?
从世俗化的意义上讲,西方文化教我们根据我们的“合理性”来评估我们的“安全性”。 这一框架说明了泰勒的说法,即所有现代人都投资于与这些虔诚的基督教观念相对应的人。 除此之外,它还提出了前一个问题: 现代被西方化的人是如何在第一时间到达最高的好?
没有最高的善,你没有标准 来证明你的理由或衡量你的圣洁。 Taylor的作品为回答这个问题提供了多张镜头,很像一个选取者在折射机中组合出一副尖锐的图像. 让我们关注其中之一:泰勒关于超好的想法。
只有当终极之地属于上帝时,普通的商品才能被释放出来,成为他们所应有的. “美好生活”为什么很难在“自我来源”第3章“Inarticulacy的道德”中定义,泰勒认为,现代西方人认为“美好生活”的概念很难理解,原因有几个。
我们的身份有许多层层,以难以言出必行的方式相互交流。 我们认识到,这些层次中有些是普遍性的,例如抽象的政治或意识形态承诺,它们也构成了其他人民的特性。 我们认识到,其他层面对我们自己来说是极为特殊的。
我们目前的身份也由我们努力叙述的长期而复杂的历史事态发展所决定,或者我们完全忽视这些事态发展。 想象一下被问到“你成为一位英国基督徒意味着什么?” 然后用“大约在AD 600年左右,肯特的异教国王Aethelberht皈依基督教......”开始回答。
你终于在2026年来到你的生活。 或者想象一下不要从Aethelberht开始, 这不是我们常做的。
Taylor确定了无艺术性伦理学的另一个因素,一个他在"世俗时代"中发展得更充分的因素:生活在超越性框架与活在永恒框架之间的区别. 自我来源是这种区别的准备阶段,但这种区别已经在那里出现。
考虑一个启蒙前,喀特斯前人,前现代人,如中世纪的欧洲人. 他以这样的方式体验了自己的自觉,以至于他认为他的思想符合事物,而不是符合他的思想. 他的道德框架因地制宜地认为,一切事物都充满了固有的意义和神圣的秩序,而宇宙整体存在于一个超越它的命令上.
这是在超乎寻常的框架内生活 它引导生命 围绕一个适当的区分 许多东西是相对的 和一件事 是本体论的终极。 终极绝对不同于平凡的,非终极的事物. 在基督教中,这表达了造物主和生物之间的区别: 一是终相相相相相相相相相相相相相相相相相相相相.
在"世俗时代"(A Secular Age)中,泰勒将从中世纪到现代的转变追溯为从超越性框架的生活到永生的转变. 在一个无穷无尽的框架里,事物符合我的思想,我的自我感从根本上从我的身体,从我的物理环境,以及任何对元物理现实的宣称中缓冲.
我区分最终事物和普通事物的方式也发生了转变,因为最终事物不再具有超越性. 这实在是一成不变。 终极作为另一个绝对超凡的现实已经消失. 相反的,我从永恒的王国, 从我身边的东西, 把它当作我的终极事物。
泰勒认为这对现代人来说是不可回避的:我们都有终极成就。 他使用“你在海上没有的东西”的语言。 如果这东西不把我的身份放在一起, 我会迷路的。
那么,核心问题是,现代世俗化的自我—— 泰勒在别处称之为在一成不变的框架中被缓冲的自我—— 如何达到最高的善? 泰勒给我们一个特别有用的镜头。 Taylor和Hypergood Taylor在《自我来源》第3章中提出了“自我来源”的概念,并在第4章“道德来源”中继续加以发展。 有两点需要注意。
首先,超好品只出现在Self源中。 泰勒在后来的作品中并没有重现它. 第二,泰勒作品的学者们以不同的方式解读了这一概念. 例如,查尔斯·布拉特伯格(Charles Blattberg)认为"超古德"是书中一个不发达的概念. 我本人的解读更接近荷兰哲学家贾斯珀·范·布伦的解读。
这个想法是这样运作的:每个人都生活在道德框架内,无论我们为阐明这个概念付出了多少努力,没有人生活在没有价值判断的道德框架内。 没有人是绝对的相对主义者, 生活需要我们找到一些比其他更重要的东西.
没有这些,我们将完全被世界的多面性所压倒和瘫痪。 我们的代理意识将结束,我们将完全被动地采取行动,但却无法采取行动。 现代人一般不会这样生活。 泰勒描述了现代人如何常常持有日益重要商品的等级.
对一些人来说,高级商品将是理性自管,家庭生活,自我表达,或名声的理想. 他写道,我们大多数人不仅生活 与很多商品, 发现我们必须排序, 在某些情况下,这种排名 使其中之一 至高无上

title: 40 Great Films for Christian Parents to Watch With Their Kids
summary: These excellent movies are enjoyable for families to watch together, but they’re also rich with values Christian parents can get behind.
summary_zh: 基督教家庭应该担心那些被称为“爱孩子”但却以精神上不健康的方式组建孩子的无数选择。 作为四个孩子的爸爸,我对斗争很了解 无法跟上向孩子们推销新电影和电视节目的内容传送带。 基督教家长需要值得信赖的馆长, 他们可以可靠地引导我们去娱乐, 这份名单是我在这场斗争中帮助基督教同胞父母的尝试. 下面的电影都是G级或PG级的,一般是“整个家庭的安全”,尽管父母仍应查阅在线内容指南,以了解他们特定家庭是否合适。
title_zh: 适合基督徒父母与孩子一起观看的40部优秀电影
content: In today’s glutted, morally compromised streaming-media environment, Christian families are right to worry about the countless options billed as “kid-friendly” but actually form kids in spiritually unhealthy ways. As a dad of four young kids, I know the struggle well. It’s impossible to keep up with the content conveyor belt of new film and TV options being marketed to kids. Christian parents need trusted curators who can reliably point us to entertainment that isn’t just “safe” for our kids to watch but is actively promoting laudable themes and (sometimes accidentally) modeling Christian virtue. This list is my attempt to help my fellow Christian parents in this struggle. The movies below are all G- or PG-rated and generally “safe for the whole family,” though parents should still consult online content guides to discern the appropriateness for their particular family. But the films I selected go beyond just safe . I commend them not only for what they don’t depict but for what they do. These movies are fun, well-made, and enjoyable for families to watch together ; they’re also rich with values Christian parents can get behind. These movies are rich with values Christian parents can get behind. I divided the list into two halves for different age groups: 20 films that might be better for your younger kids (9 and younger), and 20 films perhaps more appropriate for older kids (10 and older). If you have school-age kids, consider working your way through this list—making time not just to watch the movie together but also to discuss it afterward. Try to tease out the values and virtues the films celebrate. Cultivate in your kids a way of watching media wisely that might just become intuitive for them, with enough practice. To Watch with Younger Kids (9 and Younger) Beauty and the Beast (1991). For my money, this is the greatest of the great movies from the Disney animation heyday. The songs, the artistry, the themes of beauty, sacrifice, and love’s power to transform . . . the whole package is elegant and stately, with little of the “follow your heart” expressive individualism that compromises other Disney films of the era. Rated G. Cinderella (1950). Another all-time great Disney animated movie, the 1950 Cinderella is a gorgeous classic full of theological resonance. At a time when fairy tales and traditional romances are ridiculed or “modernized” in ways that blur moral lines, kids need the old stories where chivalric love is embraced and “happily ever after” endings aren’t pitched as problematic. Rated G. Coyote vs. Acme (2026). The newest release on this list, Coyote vs. Acme is one of the most enjoyable animated movies I’ve seen in years. Parents will laugh out loud at the satire and constant nostalgic callbacks, and kids will enjoy the vintage Looney Tunes physical humor. But more than just popcorn fun, this movie also celebrates unlikely friendship and perseverance in fighting for justice. Rated PG. David (2025). With animation as beautiful as any Disney or Pixar movie, this Angel Studios production about the biblical David blew my expectations away and landed on my top 10 list in 2025 . Biblically faithful and artistically excellent (the songs are catchy!), David has become a staple in our family’s rewatchable-movie diet. Rated PG. Despicable Me (2010). The Despicable Me franchise is one of my family’s favorites, and the first installment is rife with redemptive themes Christians can applaud. It’s the story of a hardened supervillain Gru (Steve Carell) who is morally transformed through the process of adopting three orphaned girls. Instead of the “good guy turns bad” trope that’s everywhere in pop culture, this is a “bad guy becomes better” story. Refreshing. Rated PG. Finding Nemo (2003). This is peak Pixar on both a storytelling and thematic level. The undersea adventure is visually stunning. But the film’s thematic explorations and insights for parenting are even richer. It’s a celebration of a father’s love for his son—which sometimes looks like zealous protectiveness and sometimes like letting kids learn lessons in freedom. Rated G. Homeward Bound: The Incredible Journey (1993). This lovable movie, about two dogs and a cat who band together to find their way home, was a staple of my childhood—and still holds up. It’s a classic hero’s journey, highly entertaining but also full of good lessons about perseverance, loyalty, family, and maturity. Rated G. How to Train Your Dragon (2010). This DreamWorks Animation triumph (recently remade as a “live-action” film) tells a fun story of a Viking boy who befriends and tames what should be his sworn enemy: a dragon. It’s a movie about the power of friendship to overcome fear. Rated PG. The Incredibles (2004). Brad Bird’s animated family superhero movie is one of several standouts from the golden age of Pixar (roughly 2001–2010) that made this list. I love how the movie celebrates the nuclear family, showing how a healthy, loving family unit becomes its own “superpower” greater than the sum of its parts. Rated PG. The Lion King (1994). I showed this movie to my kids for the first time recently, and they were utterly compelled. A generation after its release, The Lion King holds up as one of Disney’s 1990s animated masterpieces. The story is Shakespearean in scope and full of lessons in fortitude, justice, and choosing costly duty over carefree comfort. Rated G. Mary Poppins (1964) and Mary Poppins Returns (2018). The original Mary Poppins (starring Julie Andrews) and the recent sequel (starring Emily Blunt) are both immensely entertaining. They are also family-friendly and generally family- affirming musicals (aside from Mrs. Banks singing about how men are stupid). Arguably the original film represents a subversive critique of modernity . If your family hasn’t yet watched these classics together, make this duo a holiday-season double feature. Rated G and PG. The Muppet Christmas Carol (1992). Charles Dickens’s 1843 novella has been adapted many times, but the Muppet version is arguably the best. Faithful to the moral lessons of Dickens’s story but also just a lot of fun, this holiday classic celebrates the generous spirit of Christmas in the most wonderful ways. Rated G. Paddington series (2014, 2017, 2024). Paddington is perhaps the greatest “trilogy” ever in the kids’ movie genre. These movies are funny, sweet, and full of good lessons about family, bravery, and doing the right thing. They’re also just joyful, aesthetically vibrant, and clever in ways that appeal to all ages. Rated PG. The Peanuts Movie (2015). More kids today should be watching Peanuts cartoons. I try to annually show my kids It’s the Great Pumpkin , Charlie Brown and A Charlie Brown Christmas (both are on Apple TV). The Peanuts Movie captures the vintage, wholesome feel of the 1960s classics. Rated G. Pinocchio (1940). This is one of Disney’s earliest, and still most beloved, animated classics. The fairy tale is whimsical, at times dark, but rife with theological allusions. Its central question—what does it mean to be “real boy”?—has never been timelier and provides an entry point for a conversation parents can have with kids about humanity in an age of robots. Rated G. The Prince of Egypt (1998). The Exodus story is inherently cinematic, and the DreamWorks Animation classic remains a stunner. The artistry of the animation is at times jaw-dropping, and the story ( while not perfect ) is largely faithful to the biblical source material. Rated PG. Swiss Family Robinson (1960). This is a great movie to watch for all families, but especially if you have young boys. As the classic Disney film depicts the adventures of the shipwrecked Robinson family, it celebrates resourcefulness, teamwork, chivalry, and manly strength channeled toward providing and protecting. They don’t make virtuous adventure movies like this anymore. Rated G. Toy Story 1, 2, 3, and 5 (1995, 1999, 2010, 2026). The Toy Story movies are varying degrees of excellent

title: Why Christianity Explains Our Deepest Longings
summary: ‘Why Christianity Makes Sense’ offers a compelling argument that Christianity explains the condition of both the world and the human heart.
summary_zh: 在整个教会历史中,上帝一直唤起忠实的声音,向每一代人讲福音. 使徒保罗出行于许多已知的世界,在犹太会堂和公共场合传教. 在雅典,他把文化所问的问题作为宣示福音的平台. 类似地,奥古斯丁,安塞尔姆,布莱斯·帕斯卡尔,C.
title_zh: 为什么基督教能够解释我们最深切的渴望
content: Throughout church history, God has raised up faithful voices to speak the gospel to each generation. The apostle Paul traveled through much of the known world, preaching in synagogues and public settings. In Athens, he used the questions the culture was asking as a platform from which to proclaim the gospel. Similarly, Augustine, Anselm, Blaise Pascal, C. S. Lewis, Tim Keller, and many others helped readers see Christianity’s coherence amid the questions and assumptions of their times. Through his online ministry, Truth Unites , Gavin Ortlund fills that sort of role in our cultural moment. In Why Christianity Makes Sense: A Book About Jesus, the Mysteries of the World, and the Longings in Your Heart , Ortlund offers an accessible defense of the faith for readers unsure whether Christianity can withstand serious examination. It’s also a useful tool for discipling believers bombarded with hard questions about Christianity on the internet. Ortlund’s goal is to show “why it makes sense to be a Christian” (xiii). Ortlund’s particular strength is that he recognizes our questions aren’t merely intellectual. They arise from deeper longings for meaning, purpose, and transcendence. Unknown God In Athens, Paul thoughtfully noticed an altar established “to the unknown god” (Acts 17:23). He didn’t mock them for it. Every generation builds an altar of its own. Augustine called it the restless heart; Lewis called it Sehnsucht , the longing that joy itself cannot satisfy. Keller called the traces it leaves behind clues . Ortlund has a name for it: “the ache.” Ortlund doesn’t begin with a technical exposition of the ache but by showing it’s the desire behind every altar to every unknown god. He asks, “Are you genuinely curious about what life means—why you’re here, and what it’s all for?” (xi). The ache is the restless longing for the transcendent that we can’t put into words. Just as hunger implies we live in a world where food is meant to fuel our bodies, so the desire for meaning points to the existence of something that will satisfy that desire. So many counterfeits promise to satisfy our desire for God. Many people have learned to deny any sense of longing for the divine or simply scroll past the question before it finishes loading in their minds. Just as hunger implies we live in a world where food is meant to fuel our bodies, so the desire for meaning points to the existence of something that will satisfy that desire. In a culture where the most shocking content on social media becomes boring, it’s worth drawing attention to Jesus’s radical claims. “He claimed to be the way, the truth, and the life,” notes Ortlund. “Muhammad taught the five pillars, Buddha spoke of enlightenment, Confucius pointed to the Way, but Jesus pointed to himself as the answer. In fact, Jesus claimed to be God” (104). The claim is preposterous, unless it’s true. So Ortlund asks his readers to put on their thinking caps: “What if God is real, and Jesus is this God, showing up in history to reveal himself to us? Why not? Is it really all that much crazier than the alternatives?” (104). It’s not. And more importantly, the solution Jesus offers is the most complete answer to the ache. This message deserves to be proclaimed in public. In the Marketplace When Paul was in Athens, he “reasoned . . . in the marketplace” (Acts 17:17), the agora, which is where ideas were exchanged. Our modern agora is increasingly virtual, less of a town square and more like the comment section of a microvlog. Ortlund has excelled in this space, making hard things plain in his videos without making them small. His talent for public communication comes through in this book. For example, Ortlund tackles divine hiddenness: Have you ever wondered why, if God is indeed real, his existence isn’t completely obvious? Why are religious matters so ambiguous ? Wouldn’t a loving God want to make things clear to us? (176) It’s an intuitive argument that undermines the sense that the ache is a longing that can be fulfilled by God. There are people who have really been yearning for truth whose “years of unanswered prayers have stacked up” (177). It can be hard to explain why their search hasn’t been more fruitful. Yet we don’t have to invent answers on our own. Ortlund draws from historical sources like Pascal to argue that “partial revelation of God is a necessary feature of Christian theology.” Ortlund continues, “This is the drama of the gospel: A God who sneaks into his creation as one person within it, but who came in a manger amidst the donkeys rather than with fanfare and trumpets” (178). God has given us enough evidence of his existence; we just don’t always believe it. Our biggest problem isn’t ignorance; it’s sin. So even if everything that could be known about God was as plain as day, we might still hate him in our pride. Thus, Ortlund concludes, “A true relationship with God requires humility, which is better served by diligent searching in a partial revelation” (184). Hiddenness, with the Christian God, is an invitation to be found. Ortlund’s gift is making this complex argument clear and compelling in a few pages that a teenager can read on his phone. Some Believed Paul had to preach in Athens because his audience had never heard of the gospel. After he told the crowd about Jesus’s resurrection, some mocked, some asked to hear more, but some believed. Our biggest problem isn’t ignorance; it’s sin. Our job isn’t to make people believe but to present the truth to them in an intelligible way. Ortlund shows Christians how to do that in Why Christianity Makes Sense , which is a reader-accessible highlight reel of his more academically geared book, Why God Makes Sense in a World That Doesn’t . This book is an ideal resource to put in the hands of a college student, away from home and all that’s familiar. It will help people seeking God to know him better—or maybe for the first time. The reflection questions at the end of each chapter make it suitable for personal study or within a small-group environment. Why Christianity Makes Sense offers a compelling argument that Christianity explains the condition of both the world and the human heart.
content_zh:
在整个教会历史中,上帝一直唤起忠实的声音,向每一代人讲福音. 使徒保罗出行于许多已知的世界,在犹太会堂和公共场合传教. 在雅典,他把文化所问的问题作为宣示福音的平台. 类似地,奥古斯丁,安塞尔姆,布莱斯·帕斯卡尔,C. S.
刘易斯,蒂姆·凯勒(Tim Keller)和其他许多人帮助读者在其时代的问题和假设中看到了基督教的一致性. Gavin Ortlund通过他的网络部,
Ortlund为读者提供信仰的可及辩护, 也是一种有用的工具,
Ortlund的目标是显示“为什么成为基督徒是有意义的”(十三)。 Ortlund的特长在于他承认我们的问题不仅仅是知识。 它们产生于对意义、目的和超越的更深的渴望。 在雅典,不知名之神,保罗深思熟虑地注意到一个“对不知名之神”设立的祭坛(第17:23号法案)。 他并没有嘲笑他们。
每代自建坛. 奥古斯丁称它为"不安的心";刘易斯称它为"Sehnsucht",即欢乐本身无法满足的渴望. Keller把留下的线索称为"线索" Ortlund有一个名字:“痛”。 Ortlund并不是从对痛的技术性阐述开始,
他问道,“你是否真的好奇生活的意义, 我们无法言出必行。 正如饥饿意味着我们生活在一个粮食意在为我们的身体提供燃料的世界中一样,因此,对含义的渴望表明存在能够满足这种愿望的东西。
这么多假货承诺满足我们对上帝的渴望. 许多人已经学会否认任何对神的渴望感,或者简单地在问题完成后将问题卷过一卷而来,在他们脑海中注入。 正如饥饿意味着我们生活在一个粮食意在为我们的身体提供燃料的世界中一样,因此,对含义的渴望表明存在能够满足这种愿望的东西。
在社交媒体上最令人震惊的内容变得无聊的文化中, “他声称自己是道路、真理和生命。” “穆罕默德教了五柱子,佛说开悟,孔子指道,但耶稣指道自取. 事实上,耶稣自称是上帝"(104).
除非是真的, 所以,奥尔特伦德要求他的读者戴上他们的思维盖子:"如果上帝是真实的,而耶稣是这个上帝,在历史上出现来向我们暴露自己呢? 为什么不呢? 这是否真的比其他选择更疯狂?”(104)。 事实并非如此。 更重要的是,耶稣给出的解决方案是对痛楚最完整的答案.
这一信息应当公开发表。 在市场上,保罗在雅典时,他“在市场上为......辩护”(第17:17号法),即交换思想的地方。 更像是微相机的评论部分。
Ortlund在这个空间里表现得非常出色, 他的公开交流天赋在本书中通过. 例如,Ortlund处理神圣的隐性: 如果上帝是真的, 为什么他的存在并不完全明显? 为什么宗教事务如此模糊? 爱的上帝难道不想让我们明白吗?
(176) 这是一种直觉性的论点,它破坏了痛感是上帝能够实现的渴望。 有些人真正渴望的是真理,他们“多年的未经答复的祈祷已经堆积起来”(177年)。 很难解释为何他们的搜寻没有取得更大的成果。 但我们不必独自发明答案。
Ortlund从帕斯卡这样的历史渊源中引申出“部分启示上帝是基督教神学的一个必要特征。” Ortlund继续说,“这是福音的剧情:一个潜入他作为其中一人而创造的上帝,但他却在驴子中走来,而不是用扇子和小号来跑来”(178)。 上帝为我们提供了他存在的充分证据;
我们并不总是相信这一点。 我们最大的问题不是无知,而是罪恶。 所以,即使一切可以知道 关于上帝的 和白天一样平淡, 我们可能仍然恨他 我们的骄傲。 因此,Ortlund最后说,“与上帝的真正关系需要谦卑,如果在部分启示中勤奋地寻找,则会更好”(184)。
隐藏,与基督教神一起,是一个被找到的邀请. Ortlund的天赋在几页中使这个复杂的论点清晰而令人信服, 一些人相信保罗不得不去雅典传教,因为他的观众从未听说过福音. 他告诉了群众耶稣复活的消息后,有些人嘲笑了,有些人要求听到更多,但有些人相信.
我们最大的问题不是无知,而是罪恶。 我们的工作不是让人们相信, Ortlund 向基督徒展示如何在《基督教如何创造理智》中做到这一点,
这本书是一个理想的资源, 这将帮助人们寻求上帝,以便更了解他,或许是第一次。 每章结尾的反射问题使其适合个人学习或在小群体环境中学习.
为什么基督教让理智提出令人信服的论点,认为基督教解释世界状况和人心。
author: Thomas West

title: Using Exercise to Help Us Through the Dark Times (with Lindsey Bomgren)
summary: Fitness can be a vain, selfie-driven world. Lindsey Bomgren, founder of Nourish Move Love, shares how she found her calling there: helping women get ‘strong for their tasks’ through difficult seasons and circumstances.
summary_zh: 在"世界之角"一集中,丹·多里安尼和马克·弗罗戈普(Mark Vroegop)与"努里什移动之恋"(Nourish Move Love)的创始人林西·博姆格伦(Lindsey Bomgren)交谈,这是一家以明尼阿波利斯为基地的健身企业,花了11年时间帮助女性在家中获得力量. 一位前大学生运动员和三位母亲Lindsey在网络上打造了一个排名最高的产后锻炼计划, 她与上帝摔跤多年, Lindsey解释为什么基督徒不应该把身体当成事后思考, 她讲述了Nourish Move Love这个名字背后的故事, 要有计划,记住10分钟比零好,而贸易外观目标则是进步目标。
title_zh: 通过运动帮助我们度过黑暗时期（与Lindsey Bomgren）
content: In this episode of Your Corner of the World , Dan Doriani and Mark Vroegop talk with Lindsey Bomgren, founder of Nourish Move Love , a Minneapolis-based fitness business that has spent 11 years helping women get strong at home. A former college athlete and a mother of three, Lindsey built one of the internet’s top-ranked postpartum workout programs, and she wrestled with God for years over whether a career in fitness could serve anyone at all. Lindsey explains why Christians shouldn’t treat their bodies as an afterthought, drawing on Proverbs 31 (“Her arms are strong for her tasks,” NIV), Paul’s words on physical training and godliness, and the parable of the talents. She tells the story behind the name Nourish Move Love, opens up about a dark postpartum season that gave her new empathy for struggling women, and offers practical encouragement for beginners: Have a plan, remember that 10 minutes is better than zero, and trade appearance-based goals for progress-based ones. She also describes the long grind of building a business by giving her content away, and the burnout that led her to rethink it. Resources Mentioned: Blue Ocean Strategy by W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne The Body Teaches the Soul by Justin Whitmel Earley Habits of the Household by Justin Whitmel Earley

title: Small-Church Elders, Here’s How to Give Your Pastor a Sabbatical
summary: Our church has 74 members and two lay elders. Here’s how we raised up five men to preach seven expository sermons and give our pastor a summer sabbatical.
summary_zh: “六年前,他应该有一个安息日。 ” “我知道,”我说。 “我们知道他需要,但我们如何做到这一点? 我们有全职工作和年轻家庭。
title_zh: 小型教会的长老们，以下是为你们的牧师安排安息假的方式
content: “He should have had a sabbatical six years ago,” my fellow elder said. “I know,” I said. “We know he needs it, but how are we going to do this? We have full-time jobs and young families.” “Well, the cattle on thousand hills are the Lord’s. Let’s ask him to provide it.” I nodded in agreement, but honestly, cattle felt like less of an ask for our church. Our church consists of 74 members. We have one full-time pastor and two lay elders. And yet, exactly two years after that initial elders’ meeting, we managed to give our pastor a much-needed, six-week summer sabbatical. Five male members of our church delivered seven expository and Christ-exalting sermons. God was glorified, our pastor rested, and our church loved it. We preached through an entire book of the Bible (Habakkuk). We preached a doctrinal sermon from our confession of faith (on baptism and Communion). Two men preached for the first time. The men ranged from age 20 to 46, and I was the seasoned preacher with 25 sermons under my belt. So how did we pull this off? 1. We prayed. We knew we couldn’t do this. Only God could. This reality framed our prayers over the next two years. God was glorified, our pastor rested, and our church loved it. We came to realize that just as the Sabbath was a gift from God to man (Mark 2:27), so a sabbatical is a gift from God to a pastor. As lay elders, we were called to take steps of faith to this end while relying on the Holy Spirit’s leading and enablement. Just as Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath (Matt. 12:8), so too is he Lord of a sabbatical. As we began to make plans, we prayed that we’d hold them with an open hand and continually lay them at the feet of Jesus. We borrowed words from Jehoshaphat (2 Chron. 20:12) for our prayer in this season: “Lord, we do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you.” 2. We planned backward. We began by identifying the ideal time of year for the sabbatical. We landed on July and August, since that’s when church programming is minimal and vacations are in vogue among our congregation. This decision indirectly led us to the length of sabbatical we felt could responsibly plan for: six weeks. From there, we planned backward. The first Sunday we discussed was the Sunday our pastor would return. How did we want our brother and his wife to reintegrate into the church? We decided we wanted him to feel the warmth of our church’s love in his homecoming without being distracted by sermon preparation. So we chose to begin and end his sabbatical on Fridays. This meant our pastor had a workweek before leaving, so he could help with administrative functions. And by returning from the sabbatical on a Friday, he’d be able to join us for an elder meeting to get updates on members prior to attending church two days later. Preaching could wait another week. We created a two-year timeline that included all of the specific events and developments we thought could be feasible with the Lord’s help. This timeline helped us to answer several looming questions: Should we start the sabbatical by sending our pastor somewhere to create physical and emotional separation between him and our congregation? We agreed we should. We also felt this was an opportunity to invite our church to be generous and to tangibly show their love to our pastor of 12 years and his wife by paying for this trip. How many of our male members would be willing to assist with the preaching? We estimated three to four. How and when would we get them trained? This was the hardest question to answer but also the most rewarding part of this process. 3. We created a brotherhood. We realized our biggest hurdle would be recruiting and training men to aid in the preaching. To address the issue, we settled on offering a six-week preaching cohort during the summer prior to the sabbatical. To identify potential men for the cohort, we asked, “Which men currently do Scripture readings and prayers exceptionally well in our worship services?” Then we talked to each man individually and presented the idea for the cohort—but not yet the larger idea of supporting a future sabbatical. That would stay between us and the Lord for now. The cohort was framed as a brotherhood of men who had never preached but who would learn together. The shared adventure and even shared suffering of learning to preach a sermon made the process more appealing to the men than we anticipated. Yet, as we expected, they were also hesitant to step forward for such a public ministry. Some men had experience in regular public speaking. Others had none outside of an occasional reading and prayer humbly offered in our small church. 4. We prioritized faithfulness. As we gently navigated these discussions and tried to encourage these brothers, we realized we were missing an opportunity to remind them and ourselves that our heavenly Father’s desire for them in this process was faithfulness (1 Cor. 4:2). If that was all the man could provide us, it would be enough for God to be pleased. We didn’t hide the reality that preparing an expository sermon takes time and would cost these brothers. But we also shared about the profound, heart-shaping privilege of wrestling with a text in the power of the Holy Spirit. We described being transformed by Scripture as you labor to string sentences together in a manuscript. We encouraged. We were honest. We prayed. Before we knew it, our cohort was full. 5. We began preaching. By then, my fellow lay elder was preaching too. He and I began sending our sermon manuscripts to the men of the cohort to invite their feedback prior to preaching. We all learned through this process. We also recorded videos with our pastor where he explained his sermon-preparation process as well as the joys and hardships of preaching. These videos encouraged the men that they too could preach a sermon with God’s help and by submitting to the process we had laid before them. We shared about the profound, heart-shaping privilege of wrestling with a text in the power of the Holy Spirit. We encouraged. We were honest. We prayed. During the cohort, we gave each man Haddon Robinson’s Biblical Preaching and David Helm’s Expositional Preaching . The combination of these two books provided a hand-holding (Robinson) and theologically robust (Helm) approach to sermon writing that was helpful for a layman. We helped the men wrestle with textual observations in their Scripture passages. We taught them how to engage with different English Bible translations, commentaries, systematic theology, and biblical theology. The men labored to understand the difference between an exegetical and homiletical outline and how to use an application grid. They fumbled forward. We laughed together. We encouraged. God was glorified. At the end of six weeks, two of the men preached on an early Saturday morning to the cohort and to our pastor. A week later, one of those brothers preached the first cohort sermon in our church service. It was beautiful, and it was obvious that God was doing something in our church through these men. Epilogue These few but faithful men would go on to serve as the core preaching team for seven glorious Sundays this past summer. As a result, our pastor rested, a new generation of lay preachers was trained, and our church learned to feast on God’s Word regardless of who was preaching. Several visitors to our church during the sabbatical have since become regular attenders because of the rotation of men who faithfully preached Christ. This was a humbling and challenging process for our church, but it was also a faith-building process. It was so worth it. We’re already looking forward to the next sabbatical in a few years. Fellow lay elders, by the grace of God, in his power, and for his glory, you can give your pastor the sabbatical he needs. God desires it for your pastor, he desires it for your church, and he desires it for you. Start praying now.
content_zh:
“六年前,他应该有一个安息日。” “我知道,”我说。 “我们知道他需要,但我们如何做到这一点? 我们有全职工作和年轻家庭。” " 千山上牛是主的. 让我们请他提供。 我点头同意,但说实话, 牛感觉没有要求我们的教堂。 我们的教堂由74名会员组成.
我们有一位全职牧师和两位无业长老。 然而,在最初的长老会议两年之后,我们设法给我们的牧师一个急需的六周的暑假。 我们教会的5名男性成员进行了7次宣讲会和基督赞美会的布道会。 上帝被赞美,我们的牧师休息, 我们的教会很喜欢它。 我们通过一本《圣经》(哈巴克库克)来宣扬。
我们通过信仰的忏悔(洗礼和圣餐)来进行理论布道。 二人初传道. 这些人的年龄从20岁到46岁不等,我是老练的布道家,我的腰带下有25个布道。 我们怎么做到的? 1. 我们祈祷。 我们知道我们不能这样做。 只有上帝会 这一现实使我们在接下来的两年里祈祷。
上帝被赞美,我们的牧师休息, 我们的教会很喜欢它。 我们意识到,正如安息日是上帝送给人的礼物(马克2:27)一样,安息日是上帝送给牧师的礼物. 作为普通的长者,我们被要求为此而采取信仰步骤,同时依靠圣灵的领导和力量。 犹如耶稣是安息日的主一样。
12: 8),他也是安息日的主. 当我们开始计划时, 我们祈祷我们用开阔的手抓住他们, 我们在本季的祈祷中借用了Jehoshaphat(2 Chron. 20:12)的话,他说:我们的主啊!我们不知道该怎么办,但我们的眼睛在注视着你。 2. 我们计划落后。 我们首先确定了每年安息日的理想时间。
我们于7月和8月登陆, 这一决定间接导致了我们感到可以负责任地规划六个星期的休假时间。 从那里,我们计划向后。 我们讨论的第一个星期日 是牧师回来的星期日
我们怎么希望我们的兄弟和他的妻子 重新回到教堂? 我们决定让他在返校典礼上感受到我们教会的爱意, 所以我们选择在星期五开始和结束他的安息日。 这意味着我们的牧师在离开前有一个工作周,这样他就可以帮助履行行政职能.
在两天后参加教会活动之前, 他就能和我们一起参加长老会, 传教士可以再等一个星期 我们创造了一个为期两年的时间表,其中包括了我们认为在上帝的帮助下可能可行的所有具体事件和事态发展。
这个时间表帮助我们回答了几个迫在眉睫的问题: 我们是否应该开始安息日,派牧师去某地,在肉体和情感上建立他和我们的会众之间的分离? 我们说好的 我们还觉得这是一个机会,邀请我们的教会慷慨解囊,并通过支付这次旅行的费用,向我们12年的牧师和他的妻子实际展示他们的爱意。
我们有多少男性成员愿意协助传道? 我们估计3到4个 我们如何和何时培训他们? 这是最难回答的问题,也是这一进程中最有价值的部分。 3. 我们建立了兄弟关系。 我们意识到我们的最大障碍是招募和训练人员来协助传道。
为了解决这一问题,我们决定在安息日之前的夏天提供六周的传教班。
我们问道,为了确定这群人中的潜在男子,“现在哪些人在我们的礼拜仪式中特别善于阅读和祈祷?” 然后,我们单独地与每个人交谈,并向各群体提出这个想法,但尚未提出支持未来安息日的大想法。 暂时我们和上帝之间
这群人被陷害为兄弟会,他们从未讲道,但会一起学习。 共同的冒险,甚至共同的学习布道的痛苦,使这一进程比我们预期的更吸引人。 然而,正如我们所期望的,他们也不愿意为这样一个公共部委而前进。 有些男人有定期公开演讲的经验。
其他人除了偶尔在我们的小教堂里 恭敬地阅读和祷告之外,没有其他的东西。 4. 我们优先重视忠诚。 当我们轻而易举地引导这些讨论并试图鼓励这些兄弟时,我们意识到我们没有机会提醒他们和我们自己,我们天父在这个过程中对他们的愿望是忠诚的(1 Cor. 4:2)。
如果只有这个男人能提供我们, 上帝就足够高兴了。 我们并没有掩盖现实, 准备一场解释性布道需要时间, 但我们也分享了用圣灵的力量与文字相搏的深刻而发人心的特权.
我们描述被圣经所改变 是因为你努力把句子串在一起 我们鼓励。 我们是诚实的。 我们祈祷了 在知道之前,我们的队是满的。 5. 我们开始传教。 到那时,我的老伙计也在传道 我和他开始把我们的布道稿 寄给一群人 在布道之前请他们反馈
我们都从这一进程中吸取了教训。 我们还与我们的牧师一起录制了录像,其中他解释了他的布道准备过程以及布道的喜悦和困难。 这些影片鼓励人们在上帝的帮助下,
我们分享了用圣灵的力量与文字相搏的深厚的、令人心碎的特权。 我们鼓励。 我们是诚实的。 我们祈祷了 我们给了每个人Haddon Robinson的圣经传奇和David Helm的博览会。
这两本书的结合提供了手持(Robinson)和神学上坚固(Helm)的布道方法,对外行人很有帮助. 我们帮助男人们在他们的圣经段落里 用文字观察进行斗争 我们教他们如何与不同的英语圣经翻译,评论,系统神学,和圣经神学进行接触.
男子们努力理解外观和喜剧提纲之间的区别以及如何使用应用网格. 他们向前冲 我们一起笑 我们鼓励。 上帝被赞美。 在六周后,两个男人在周六清晨 和我们的牧师讲道
一周后,其中一位兄弟在我们教会服务中 讲了第一组布道。 这是美丽的, 很明显,上帝正在做一些事情 在我们的教堂 通过这些人。 爱 这些少数但忠心耿耿的人 会继续作为核心传教团队 在7个光荣的星期日 今年夏天。
因此,我们的牧师休息了,新一代的非宗教传教士接受了培训,我们的教会学会了接受上帝的旨意,不管是谁在传教。 安息日期间,由于忠实地宣扬基督的人轮流参加,几位参观我们教堂的人从此成为了常客.
这对我们的教会来说是一个艰难而有挑战性的进程,但它也是一个建立信仰的进程。 这是如此值得的。 我们已期待几年后的下个安息日。 弟兄们 奉上帝之恩 以他的力量 为了他的荣耀 你可以给你的牧师 他需要的安息日
上帝希望它为你牧师, 他希望它为你教堂, 他希望它为你。 开始祈祷吧

title: Where Our Criminal Justice System Breaks Down (with Matt Martens)
summary: Matt Martens joins Collin Hansen to discuss justice, citizenship, and Christian responsibility.
summary_zh: 当你真的想深入到关于公共政策的大问题的细节中——我们怎样才能更好地一起生活——你遇到了两个问题: 基督徒不愿介入细节。 Matt Martens在2023年出自Crossway的"改革刑事司法:基督教建议"一书时, 今天, 马特是华盛顿特区的一家国际法公司的审判律师和合伙人. 他和妻子是Capitol Hill浸信会的成员,他们有两个儿子和一个女儿. 我读了这本书, 就在前几天,我正想着这本书, 和我的一位牧师交谈, 他准备从彼得讲正义和服从当局。
title_zh: 我们的刑事司法制度在哪些方面存在缺陷（与Matt Martens合著）
content: When you really want to dive into the details of big questions about public policy—how we can live better together—you run into two problems: The experts and other stakeholders don’t want to consider Christian arguments, and Christians don’t want to engage in the details. That combination of a Christian argument from a legal expert was rare when Matt Martens’s book Reforming Criminal Justice: A Christian Proposal came out in 2023 from Crossway. And it’s still rare today. Matt is a trial lawyer and partner at an international law firm in Washington, DC. He and his wife are members at Capitol Hill Baptist Church, and they have two sons and a daughter. I read this book when it came out, and it’s stuck with me. Just the other day, I was thinking about the book when talking to one of my pastors, who was preparing to preach from 1 Peter on justice and obeying authorities. I thought about how I’d want to see the criminal justice system reformed if there were a good shot I’d be either a victim or criminal defendant. Isn’t that the law summed up in loving our neighbors as ourselves? From the death penalty to AI to the decline of violent crime—Matt and I covered a great deal. In This Episode 00:00 – Why poor defendants often lack adequate legal representation 02:00 – The biggest misconception about the American criminal justice system 03:32 – The criminal justice reform Matt would prioritize first 07:21 – DNA evidence, wrongful convictions, and the fallibility of the system 13:26 – Why Matt opposes the death penalty as currently practiced 19:43 – Why preaching the gospel doesn’t eliminate our responsibility to pursue public justice 22:23 – Why Christians should serve on juries 27:38 – What decades as a lawyer taught Matt about how justice actually works 39:56 – Raymond Flanks: faith after nearly 39 years of wrongful imprisonment 46:26 – How AI could transform legal work and expand access to justice Resources Mentioned: Reforming Criminal Justice by Matthew T. title: The Cumulative Effect of Thousands of Family Bible Times
summary: When your kids are inattentive or disruptive, don’t be overly discouraged. If the milk spills, if a fight erupts, all is not lost.
summary_zh: 警报响起,另一个忙碌的日子开始了。 让孩子们起床准备上学 准备吃饭 工作 课后活动 在你还没知道之前 日子就要结束了 你又筋疲力尽了。 作为基督徒的父母,我们希望我们的生命 成为基督。 我们真诚地希望我们的儿童也为基督而活。
title_zh: 数千次家庭圣经时间的累积效应
content: The alarm goes off, and another busy day begins. Getting kids up and ready for school, meal prep, work, after-school activities. Before you know it, the day is racing to its close. And you’re exhausted again. As Christian parents, we want our lives to count for Christ. We sincerely want our children to live their lives for Christ too. We want them to be changed by the same amazing grace that has transformed us. But how does this happen? How can we find the time and energy to effectively disciple our kids? Where will we find the creativity and passion to teach them what matters most? If you’re discouraged by your limited time and ability to shepherd your children, consider the cumulative effects of thousands of family Bible readings over the course of many years. Think Small What if a brief Bible reading today, a couple more later this week, and a few more next week eventually became a pattern, a deeply rooted habit for your family? Small investments of time and intentionality can make a big difference over a couple decades. Small investments of time and intentionality can make a big difference over the span of a couple decades. Years ago, Trevin Wax wrote an article titled “ 1000 Sermons Will Change Your Life .” What he says to pastors about preaching also applies to parents who lead their kids in family Bible reading: Pastors, don’t underestimate the cumulative effect of your preaching. You are not dumping information into brains. You are forming the habits of your people, teaching them how to read and understand and apply the Bible for themselves. Similarly in family life, our discipleship has cumulative effects that may not come to fruition for years. As parents, we’re in this for the long haul. If your children live in your home from birth to age 18, that’s 6,570 days. If you read the Bible together on average every third day, that’s 2,190 Bible readings over the course of your sons’ and daughters’ childhood and teenage years. Keep that big picture in mind when you feel defeated after a couple days on the go, when those family discipleship moments have eluded you. Think of Timothy, who was acquainted with the sacred writings from childhood because of his mother’s and grandmother’s faithful witness (2 Tim. 1:5; 3:14–15). May we be influential parents like them, who little by little and day by day pass on our life of faith to the next generation. Be Consistent, Establish a Habit With the long view in mind, think small in terms of your goals for this week, month, or year. Aim for consistency, for establishing a habit that you can pray will take root in your kids’ lives. Joe Carter recently shared the results of a sociological study of how faith moves across generations. He summarized the findings: The behaviors that most strongly predict lasting faith are active and verbal: praying together as a family, saying grace, embedding faith in the rhythm of the week rather than reserving it for Sunday, and, above all, talking about it. Children raised in homes where faith was discussed at least several times a week were more than twice as likely to attend church, pray daily, and rate religion as very important in young adulthood. The simplest way to put this truth into practice in your home is by creating a rhythm of opening the Bible regularly, reading some verses, and discussing them. You may never have a sense that one particular devotional was transformative. But keep at it. When your kids are inattentive or disruptive, don’t be overly discouraged. If the milk spills, if a fight erupts, all is not lost. Resist the temptation to quit. Come back to the reading the next day, or the day after that. Keep finding times to open the Bible with your family. Let the Word Do the Heavy Lifting Another deterrent that may get in the way of family discipleship is “the intimidation factor.” If you feel ill-equipped to teach the Bible to your kids, you may be inclined to leave that task to Sunday school teachers and youth pastors. But you don’t have to be a Bible scholar or an expert apologist to faithfully disciple your children. When your kids are inattentive or disruptive, don’t be overly discouraged. If the milk spills, if a fight erupts, all is not lost. God’s Word is sufficient to transform their lives as they behold God’s glory the good news of Jesus Christ in its pages. Encourage your kids to ask questions. And get used to saying, “I’m not sure how to answer that question. Let’s try to figure that out together.” God is too big for us to completely understand. So focus on the basics. Share what you’ve learned. Share how you study when you don’t know the answers. And most importantly, share how Jesus has changed you personally and practically, how he has forgiven you and made you a different person than you were before. Pray Big As you think small, aim to establish a consistent habit, and let the Bible do the heavy lifting, also pray big! It’s not within our power to breathe spiritual life into our children. Only God can do that saving work, by his Spirit and through his Word. Pray with and for your children. Pray for God to take your small investments of time and multiply the effects in your kids’ lives so they come to know our great Savior and want to make him known to others. Pray for the ripple effect of these thousands of family Bible readings to be felt for decades to come.

title: Would God Ever Say, ‘I Will Save You No More’?
summary: Our hope doesn’t rest on the sincerity of our repentance, as important as that is. Our hope ultimately rests on the compassion of our God.
summary_zh: 父母知道,并不是每一个“对不起”都是相同的。 有时“对不起”的意思是“对不起我被抓了”或“对不起我面对后果”。 然而,有时这意味着“我错了。 你会原谅我吗?
title_zh: 神是否会说：“我不再拯救你了”？
content: Parents know that not every “I’m sorry” is the same. Sometimes “I’m sorry” means “I’m sorry I got caught” or “I’m sorry I’m facing the consequences.” Yet sometimes it means “I was wrong. Will you forgive me?” Parents also don’t respond to every apology the same way. Sometimes we immediately embrace our child. Other times we slow the conversation down. We ask questions. We press a little deeper, because we don’t just want to hear the words “I’m sorry.” We want those words to reflect a changed heart. In Judges 10, we encounter shocking words. The Lord says, “I will save you no more. Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you in the time of your distress” (vv. 13–14). Would God ever speak words like that to us ? Like a good parent, God knows there are different kinds of “I’m sorry,” and he’s not satisfied with words alone. He sometimes speaks to his people in surprising ways because he’s after our hearts. Lord’s Holy Rebuke The book of Judges follows a familiar pattern. Israel sins. The Lord gives them over to their enemies. They cry out. Then the Lord raises up a deliverer (e.g., 2:10–16). But that pattern isn’t merely a repeating cycle—it’s a downward spiral. Like a good parent, God knows there are different kinds of ‘I’m sorry,’ and he’s not satisfied with words alone. By Judges 10, Israel has descended deeper into idolatry than ever before. No longer content to run after the gods of the Canaanites, they’ve collected gods from every surrounding nation. Consequently, their existence hangs in the balance as their enemies move into Israel’s heartland. Yet as Israel’s sin and misery reaches a new low, their confession reaches a new height. For the first time in Judges, Israel confesses their sin (v. 10). But apparently, the Lord has heard this speech before . He knows when “I’m sorry” is little more than words. So instead of raising up another deliverer, he reminds Israel of his repeated acts of salvation (vv. 11–12). Then comes the striking statement: “I will save you no more” (v. 13). Those words should unsettle us. They certainly would’ve unsettled Israel. God’s words expose their dangerous presumption. For generations, Israel assumed the pattern would continue. They thought they could repeatedly forsake the Lord and simply return to him whenever life became unbearable. But not this time. The Lord’s rebuke shatters their assumption. You chose your gods. Cry out to them. Let them save you. The Lord exposes both their idols’ emptiness and their hearts’ audacity. Their gods cannot save them. And the Lord won’t be treated as an emergency deliverer while his people give themselves to other gods. Moreover, the Lord’s rebuke isn’t just for Israel. It’s meant to confront us today. These words were written for our instruction (1 Cor. 10:11). We also shouldn’t assume we can cling to our idols, live in our sin, ignore God’s commands, and then simply cry out to him when life falls apart. God isn’t manipulated by empty words. His rebuke exposes our idols and confronts our presumption. He calls us to repentance. Lord’s Compassion When the Lord rebukes Israel, they finally move beyond mere words to genuine repentance. They put away the foreign gods and serve the Lord (v. 16). As soon as they do, we read, “[The Lord] became impatient over the misery of Israel.” Or we might translate it, “He could bear Israel’s suffering no longer” (v. 16, JB). One of the most shocking verses in Judges is followed by one of its most beautiful. The God who rightly opposes sin is also moved by his people’s suffering. The God who says “I will save you no more” is the same God who only bears his people’s misery for so long. Certainly, this passage calls for genuine repentance. Yet when it explains God’s response, it doesn’t point us first to Israel’s motivation but to God’s . It doesn’t say, “Israel’s heart was finally sincere.” It says, “[The LORD] became impatient over the misery of Israel.” Our hope doesn’t rest on the sincerity of our repentance, as important as that is. Our hope ultimately rests on the compassion of our God. We need both parts of this passage. If we’ve grown comfortable with sin and presume on God’s grace, we need God’s holy rebuke. But if we’re crushed beneath the weight of our failures, if we know our repentance falls short and wonder if God is finished with us, then we need a reminder that the God who refuses to overlook sin also refuses to bear his people’s misery forever. God’s compassion moves him to save. Holiness and Compassion of the Cross This tension we feel between God’s holiness and his compassionate love finds its fulfillment at the cross. There, God’s holiness wasn’t set aside—and neither was his compassion. At the cross, God’s holy rebuke fell. His wrath was poured out—but not on us. Instead, it fell on his Son. God’s compassion was displayed as the sinless One bore the full rebuke our sin deserves that we might receive the love we never deserved. Our hope doesn’t rest on the sincerity of our repentance, as important as that is. Our hope ultimately rests on the compassion of our God. Then, after rising from the dead, Christ pours out his Spirit on us, renews our hearts, and enables us to do what Israel never fully did—put away our idols and serve the Lord. Parents know that “I’m sorry” isn’t always the same. Our Heavenly Father knows too. He refuses to settle for empty words. Yet when his people truly return to him, they don’t find a reluctant Father. They find a God rich in mercy. Let’s return to the Lord whose holy rebuke leads us to repentance and whose compassionate love moves him to save.

父母知道,并不是每一个“对不起”都是相同的。 有时“对不起”的意思是“对不起我被抓了”或“对不起我面对后果”。 然而,有时这意味着“我错了。 你会原谅我吗?" 父母对道歉的反应也不相同。 有时我们马上拥抱我们的孩子。 其他时候,我们慢下来的对话。 我们问问题。
因为我们并不想听到“对不起”的话。 我们希望这些话能够反映改变的心意。 在法官10中,我们遇到令人震惊的言论。 主说:我不会再拯救你们了。 去呼喊你们所选择的神灵吧,在你们受难的时候,让他们拯救你们。” 上帝会这样对我们说话吗?
他对言语并不满意。 他有时以出人意料的方式与人民交谈, 主的圣训 法官书遵循一种熟悉的模式。 以色列的罪过 主把他们交给敌人 他们喊出。 然后,主举起一个送货人(例如2:10-16).
但这种模式不仅仅是一个重复循环,而是螺旋式的下降。 像一个好父母一样,上帝知道有不同种类的"对不起",他并不满足于单词. 根据10位法官的说法,以色列比以往更深地陷入偶像崇拜。 他们不再满足于追逐迦南人的神,
因此,当敌人进入以色列的心脏地带时,他们的存在就处于平衡之中。 然而,随着以色列的罪恶和苦难达到一个新的地步,他们的忏悔达到了一个新的地步。 以色列首次在法官中承认他们的罪过(v.10)。 但很明显,上帝以前听过这个演讲 他知道, " 我很抱歉 " 只不过是言语而已。

他们以为他们可以一再抛弃主,只要生命变得难以忍受,就干脆回到他身边. 但这次不行 主的谴责打破了他们的假设。 你选择了自己的神 哭出他们。 让他们救你 主揭露了他们的偶像的虚空和胆怯。 他们的神不能拯救他们。
主不会被当作紧急救援者, 而且,上帝的谴责不仅仅是针对以色列的。 今天, 这些文字是写给我们的指示(1 Cor. 10:11). 我们不应该认为我们可以坚持我们的偶像,
他们一来,我们就说:我们的主,就为以色列的灾难而烦躁了。 或者我们可以翻译为:"他可能不再忍受以色列的痛苦"(v.16, JB. 在法官中最令人震惊的诗句之一紧随其后的是最美丽的诗句之一。 正确反对罪恶的上帝也因人民的痛苦而感动.
说“我不会再拯救你们”的上帝就是这个只承受了人民如此之久苦难的上帝。 当然,这段话需要真正的忏悔。 但当它解释上帝的反应时, 它并不首先指向以色列的动机,
“以色列终于真心实意。 上面说:“耶和华对于以色列的苦难变得不耐烦了。” 我们的希望并不在于我们悔改的诚意, 我们的希望最终取决于我们上帝的同情。 我们需要这段话的两个部分。 如果我们对罪恶感到自在,
但是,如果我们被压在失败的重心下,如果我们知道我们的悔过是不足的,并且怀疑上帝是否与我们同归于尽,那么我们需要提醒我们,拒绝忽略罪恶的上帝也拒绝永远承受他人民的痛苦。 上帝的怜悯感动他拯救。
宗座和对十字的同情 我们感到上帝的圣洁和慈悲的爱之间的这种紧张关系在十字架上得到了实现。 在那里,上帝的圣洁没有被搁置一旁,他的同情心也没有被搁置一旁。 在十字架上,上帝的神圣责难倒地. 他的怒火被喷出,但不是我们。 相反,它落在他儿子身上。
上帝的怜悯被展现为无罪之人 我们罪孽深重 罪孽深重 我们的希望并不在于我们悔改的诚意, 我们的希望最终取决于我们上帝的同情。
然后,基督从死地复活后,将他的精神倾注在我们身上,使我们恢复心智,使我们能做以色列从未做过的事——即抛弃我们的偶像,崇拜主。 父母知道“对不起”并不总是一样。 我们的天父也知道 他拒绝为空话和解. 当他的族人真正回到他身边时,
他们发现上帝充满了仁慈 让我们回到上帝身边吧,

title: When You Need a Christmas Miracle
summary: We won’t find all our struggles tied up with a neat bow like the gifts under our trees. But God, our Immanuel, will be with us through it all.
summary_zh: 故你应当宣读,主将给你一个迹象。 看 哪 、 处 女 要 孕 育 一 个 子 子 、 起 名 叫 以 曼 奴 (以萨. 7:14 反射 如果你今年看几部节日电影, 节日的季节显然具有神奇的能力,能够把灵魂伴侣聚集在一起,拯救家庭企业并治愈无法治愈的疾病。 12月25日转来转去,不可能实现。
title_zh: 当您需要圣诞奇迹时
content: Read Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. (Isa. 7:14) Reflect If you watch even a few holiday movies this year, you’ll encounter the trope of the “Christmas miracle.” The festive season apparently has the magical ability to bring soulmates together, rescue floundering family businesses, and heal incurable diseases. The impossible becomes possible when December 25 rolls around. The nation of Judah in Isaiah’s day was in dire need of a miracle. They were in a centuries-long cycle of sin and rebellion against God. The northern kingdom of Israel had joined forces with Syria, and together they threatened to attack. Judah’s evil king, Ahaz, wouldn’t submit to God. What hope did they have? The impossible becomes possible when December 25 rolls around. Despite Ahaz’s hard-heartedness, God shows grace by making a promise: “The Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel” (Isa. 7:14). Later, in Matthew’s Gospel, we learn that “Immanuel” means “God with us” (Matt. 1:23). A spark of light appears in Judah’s dark future. But it didn’t seem like it could happen. A virgin bearing a son? Impossible. God dwelling among sinful people? Impossible. Yet this is what we celebrate at Christmas. Matthew recounts Jesus’s birth and tells us that “all this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet” (v. 22)—Christ is the ultimate fulfillment of God’s promise through Isaiah. God did the impossible. What seems impossible to you this Christmas? You may have a list of tasks, commitments, and events so long that you can’t possibly get it all done—let alone with a sense of peace, contentment, or even sanity. You may be facing family conflict, and you don’t know how to begin healing the divides. You may be grieving, and the prospect of finding any holiday joy seems remote. God doesn’t promise to do everything that seems impossible. On Christmas morning, we won’t find all our struggles tied up with a neat bow like the gifts under our trees. But God, our Immanuel, will be with us through it all. Impossible as it once seemed, God himself “came into the world to save sinners” (1 Tim. 1:15). He’s with us now by his Spirit, and one day he’ll return to make a new world and dwell with us physically and eternally. We won’t find all our struggles tied up with a neat bow like the gifts under our trees. But God, our Immanuel, will be with us through it all. So this Advent season, look to your God who does the impossible. Pray earnestly for peace and rest, for healing, for reconciliation, for joy. But remember he has already given us what we need. He’s redefined what’s impossible: “Neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8:38–39). It’s impossible that he’ll abandon us. Because God is steadfastly with us, we can face what seems insurmountable this Christmas. Our weaknesses and sins will not hinder God’s determination to save and dwell among his people. He is God with us, now and forever, as the apostle John sees in his vision of the future: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Rev. 21:3). Respond What impossible situation are you facing this Christmas? Spend time praying about that today. Consider what we learn about the Lord from these verses and how that changes the way you think about your struggles or fears. What difference does it make that God is with you?

尽管阿哈兹心狠手辣,但真主仍以一个诺言示恩: " 主自己会给你一个迹象。 处女将孕育一子并称为Immanuel”(以莎. 7:14)。 后来,在马太福音中,我们了解到 " Immanuel " 的意思是 " 神与我们同在 " (Matt.1:23)。 犹大黑暗的未来出现了一股光芒。 但似乎不可能发生。
怀有儿子的处女? 这不可能 真主必定要惩治犯罪的民众。 这不可能 这是我们在圣诞节庆祝的 Matthew讲述了耶稣的出世,并告诉我们, " 所有这一切都是为了实现先知所说的上帝的话 " (v. 22)——基督是通过以赛亚来最终实现上帝的诺言. 上帝做了不可能的事,你没有 你觉得这圣诞节不可能吗?
你可能有一份任务、承诺和事件的清单, 你可能面临家庭冲突, 你可能很伤心, 找到任何假日快乐的前景 似乎遥远。 上帝没有承诺做一切看起来不可能的事。
在圣诞节早上, 我们不会发现我们所有的挣扎 绑起一个干净的弓像 我们树下的礼物。 但上帝,我们的伊曼纽尔,将和我们一起度过这一切。 从前看来不可能,上帝自己“来到世界去拯救罪人”(1 Tim.1:15)。 他与我们同在,
我们不会发现我们所有的挣扎都与像树下礼物一样的整洁的弓捆绑在一起。 但上帝,我们的伊曼纽尔,将和我们一起度过这一切。 因此,这个宗教的季节, 看看你的上帝 谁做不可能。 诚恳地祈祷和平和休息,祈祷治愈,祈祷和解,祈祷欢乐. 但记得他已经给了我们我们需要的
他重新定义了不可能的事情 : “ 无论是死亡、生命、天使、统治者、现在的东西、未来的东西、力量、高度、深度,还是所有众生中的任何事物,都不能把我们与基督耶稣的爱分开。” 他不可能抛弃我们。
因为上帝与我们同在, 我们可以面对 似乎无法克服的这个圣诞节。 我们的弱点和罪恶不会妨碍上帝拯救自己人民并在他们中间居住的决心。 他与我们同在,现在和永远,正如使徒约翰在他对未来的展望中看到的那样:“看哪,上帝的居所与人同在。
他将与他们同住,他们将成为他的子民,而真主也作为他们的神与他们同住”(Rev.21:3)。 响应 这圣诞节你面临什么不可能的情况? 花时间祈祷今天。 想想我们从这些诗句中得知了上帝什么 以及这如何改变你对斗争或恐惧的思考 神与你同在有什么区别?
author: Cassie Achermann

title: What Roman History Can (and Can’t) Explain About Christianity
summary: ‘Rome’s Age of Revolution’ is a tightly argued book that makes a number of important connections between the Greco-Roman world and the formation of the early church.
summary_zh: 罗马革命时代的矛盾和紧张局势中,没有一个比这本书和它的尘土覆盖物的相去甚远。 这并非作者Tim Whitmarsh的过错, 出版商也从未夸大某一论文的新奇、原创性、争议甚至丑闻, 但它的罐子 尽管如此。 它产生了无法实现的期望的不幸效果, 它将一本清晰,简短,写得很好,深思熟虑, 和完全合理的书变成了一种轻微的失望。
title_zh: 罗马历史能够（和不能够）为基督教做出哪些解释
content: Of all the paradoxes and tensions in Rome’s Age of Revolution , none is so striking as the contrast between the book and its dustcover. That’s not the fault of the author, Tim Whitmarsh, currently regius professor of Greek at the University of Cambridge. Nor is it unheard of for publishers to exaggerate the novelty, originality, controversy, or even scandal of a particular thesis, especially when promoting scholarly arguments to a wider audience. But it jars nonetheless. And it has the unfortunate effect of creating undeliverable expectations, which turn a clear, brief, well-written, thoughtful, and perfectly reasonable book into a slight disappointment. “This remarkable book redefines early Christianity,” proclaims the first endorsement on the back cover. “Dazzling. This thrilling and elegantly written book will change how you see Rome, and Christianity, for ever,” says the next. The breathlessness continues. Harry Sidebottom says it “makes us rethink everything we know about the rise of Christianity.” Candida Moss commends it for “for ever changing how we think about the entanglement of empire, culture and early Christianity.” The inside jacket has fewer references to “everything” and “for ever,” but praise for the book’s originality continues: “Offers a whole new way to view Christians as an integrated part of the whole, multifaceted ancient Mediterranean world.” And so forth. There’s nothing wrong with rave reviews and ringing endorsements, of course. The problem in this case is that they lead the reader to anticipate a fresh, bold, provocative, and potentially explosive new argument, which is exactly what Rome’s Age of Revolution: Augustus, Empire, and the Making of Christianity doesn’t provide. What it offers instead is a measured, straightforward, run-of-the-mill presentation of a widely accepted view—that Christianity “was decisively and fundamentally shaped by the culture that incubated it” (228), both Greek and Roman, and “could not have come into being in anything like the form we know it without the revolutionary impact of Augustus’ political reforms” (230)—to a nonspecialist audience. Little in here is new, or claims to be. Plenty of it is found embryonically in Eusebius, Chrysostom, Thomas Aquinas, and John Calvin, to say nothing of F. F. Bruce or N. T. Wright. Integration and Conflict Whitmarsh revels in nuance, not controversy. “From one perspective, Christianity changed everything. From another, it reflected the world around it” (xxiv). It would be simplistic, for example, to frame an argument in terms of Greco-Roman cultural influence on early Christianity, because influence flows both ways. It would be equally simplistic to point out all the ways in which the ante-Nicene church aped and adapted imperial Rome without noting the ways in which they had nothing to do with each other: “There was very little that was Augustan about, for example, the Eucharist” (231). Similarly, although “most Christians were fully integrated into Roman society, and no more or less harassed than anyone else” (184), and although many stories of Christian martyrdom were stylized, embellished, or even invented, there’s no doubt that emperors like Decius and Diocletian pursued “systematic, pan-imperial action” and “vindictively anti-Christian policies” (186) and that “Christian zealots were certainly executed” (204). His analogy is apt: Although we know that the representation of cowboys and Indians in a western movie is usually a cinematic distortion, it would be a mistake to assume on that basis that conflict between settlers and indigenous peoples in North America in the nineteenth century was entirely the invention of Hollywood. (203–4) The book is at its best in parts 1 and 2, when describing the endlessly fascinating world of the late Roman republic and early Roman empire, and the ways in which it made Christianity’s message comprehensible and its expansion possible. Roman Influence on Christianity The universal access to the gospel, for instance, would’ve been hard to imagine without the award of citizenship to all free males on the Italian peninsula, which is the moment “when Roman identity ceased to be tied geographically to the city of Rome itself, and began to be associated more with loyalty to an idea” (4). The book is at its best when describing the ways in which the Roman world made Christianity’s message comprehensible and its expansion possible. The story of Luke-Acts is that of a Roman road trip, set in a world in which Homeric seaways have been replaced by Augustan highways. The paradigmatic Christian form of literature was the letter, which likewise depended on safe roads, milestones, and transport infrastructure. We could go on: Roman laws, aqueducts, bridges, provinces, and architecture all reconfigured the concept of space in ways that shaped the early Christian movement. In related ways, “Augustus’ revolution reset time as well as space” (77). The arrival of Augustus signified a new world order, complete with a new calendar centered on his person and a sense that the old age had passed and a new one arrived. Not only that, but “the earliest Christians seem to have used a characteristically Augustan approach to time” (112), regarding themselves as the fulfillment of Jewish prophecies much as (say) Virgil saw the Romans as the true heirs of Homeric Greece. Readers may quibble with Whitmarsh’s use of “supersessionism” in this context, but the comparison is fascinating and well drawn. When we situate the early church within this world, its growth, influence, and missionary strategy all make good historical sense, as Whitmarsh shows in part 3. Within Greco-Roman communities, and cities in particular, Christian leaders would have been recognizable as Charismatics, religious experimenters competing for success within a deregulated religious market; as Experts, presenting themselves as philosophers with “a coherent system of wisdom that competed with, indeed far outdid, the various Greek philosophical schools” (148); as Bibliophiles, writing and reading books because they operated in a literate world; and as Zealots, with their violent and heroic stories of martyrdom. There are even points of overlap between Greek novels and early Christian thought, once again with influence flowing in both directions. Occasional Overstatements Though the book is generally balanced in tone, occasionally it strays into overstatement or factual error. It’s a stretch to say that Jesus’s original teachings are “lost forever” because we only have them in Greek translation (xix); it’s simply untrue to say that “we do not, of course, have a single word securely attributed to Jesus, who spoke only Aramaic” (37), in light of well-known examples like “talitha koum,” “ephphatha,” “Abba,” “Cephas,” “Boanerges,” “mammon,” and “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani.” To be fair, some of Whitmarsh’s overstatements are standard fare among classicists who aren’t Christians: “The fact that the Christmas story is a fiction is well understood, and has been for hundreds of years” (92). Though the book is generally balanced in tone, occasionally it strays into overstatement or factual error. But some overstatements are more surprising and would be rejected by many in the scholarly guild: “It is a theme central to the theology of the Gospels: that the coming of Jesus . . . renders Jewish law obsolete” (111). Equally puzzling is his belief that Christians only met in private homes, not least because it comes right after citing a work (by my doctoral supervisor, no less) that demonstrates the reverse to be true. Some errors are inexplicable, especially for a professor of Greek. His claim that “slave” is the dominant meaning of diakonos in the Septuagint (144) is completely upside down; diakonos only appears a handful of times, and never to translate eved , for which the translators usually use doulos or pais . More baffling still is the idea that the author of 1 Corinthians 7:3–5 was characte
content_zh:
罗马革命时代的矛盾和紧张局势中,没有一个比这本书和它的尘土覆盖物的相去甚远。 这并非作者Tim Whitmarsh的过错,
出版商也从未夸大某一论文的新奇、原创性、争议甚至丑闻, 但它的罐子 尽管如此。
它产生了无法实现的期望的不幸效果, 它将一本清晰,简短,写得很好,深思熟虑, 和完全合理的书变成了一种轻微的失望。 “这本杰出的书重新定义了早期的基督教,”在背面上宣布了第一次认可。 “令人惊叹。
这本令人兴奋而优雅的书将改变你对罗马和基督教的看法。” 气息相续.
Harry Sidebottom说“让我们重新思考我们对基督教兴起的一切了解。 坎地达 摩斯称赞它“永远改变我们对帝国、文化和早期基督教缠绕的思考方式 ” 。 内部夹克很少提到"一切"和"永远",但对该书原创性的赞美继续: "用全新的方式将基督徒视为一个直觉"
整个多元的古地中海世界的一部分。” 等诸相. 当然,
问题在于它们让读者预见到一个新的、大胆的、挑衅性的和潜在的爆炸性的新论点,这正是罗马革命时代:奥古斯都、帝国和基督教的造就所不能提供的。
相反,它所提供的是一种有分寸、直截了当、一而再而再而三地提出的一种广泛接受的观点,即基督教 " 是由它所孕育的文化决定性和根本地塑造的 " (228年),希腊语和罗马语,以及 " 没有奥古斯都政治改革的革命影响,不可能以我们所知道的形式出现 " (230年)——对一个非专家学者来说。

例如,从Greco-Roman文化对早期基督教的影响的角度来设定一个论点是简单化的,因为影响是双向流动的。
